title: systemd-boot fails to prepare large initrd with Bad Buffer Size on Dell R420 firmware
body: I am running systemd 252 on Arch Linux with kernel 6.1.1-arch1-1 on an x86_64 Dell R420. After selecting my systemd-boot entry, boot fails with “Error preparing initrd: Bad Buffer Size.” The ESP is FAT32 mounted at /boot, with the kernel and initramfs stored there. This setup worked for about two years but has become flaky over the last few weeks or months. Reinstalling and rebuilding boot components briefly made it work, but the failure returned. I had also been experimenting with unified kernel images and EFI boot entries and briefly ran out of NVRAM space.

symptoms_visible: After I select the Arch Linux entry in systemd-boot, boot stops with “Error preparing initrd: Bad Buffer Size.”
The same setup worked for about two years, but recently the boot failure has become intermittent and then persistent.
N0.label: N0 initrd preparation failure reported

symptoms_visible: The initrd files have nonzero sizes in the EFI shell.
Boot succeeds when I remove the loader entry's initrd directives and put the initrd paths in the kernel command line instead; using the loader initrd directives still produces “Bad Buffer Size.”
N1.label: N1 kernel-side initrd loading works

symptoms_visible: The debug boot build still stops while preparing the initrd and prints “Bad Buffer Size.”
I tested with the fallback initrd, and the regular initrd fails through the loader directives as well.
N2.label: N2 firmware read failure captured

symptoms_visible: During the kernel-side probe with the large initrd and efi=nochunk, the boot screen also reports a Bad Buffer Size failure.
N3.label: N3 large single-read probe reproduced failure

symptoms_visible: The automatic chunk-size test prints different results as it tries a sequence of read sizes; the complete console output is captured in my PiKVM screenshots.
N4.label: N4 chunk-size behavior measured

symptoms_visible: With the build that retries by reopening the initrd after the large read, boot still stops with the same “Bad Buffer Size” message.
N4_x.label: N4_x reopen-and-retry attempt aftermath

symptoms_visible: The debug build prints the expected and returned initrd sizes and a SHA-256 value during boot; I also captured the corresponding sha256sum output after booting through my workaround.
N5.label: N5 reopened-file corruption evidence collected

symptoms_visible: The latest candidate build boots the original loader entry successfully; the initrd preparation error is gone.
N6.label: N6 corrected candidate verified

symptoms_visible: The system boots normally from the systemd-boot entry with its initrd directives, and “Error preparing initrd: Bad Buffer Size” no longer appears.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved with chunked initrd reads

question_patterns: Can you check the kernel and initrd sizes from the EFI shell and confirm that none of the referenced files has size zero?
What sizes does the EFI shell report for the files referenced by this loader entry?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: They look OK in the EFI shell; neither initrd is empty. I attached photos of the file listings and sizes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: One of the referenced initrd files is actually zero bytes in the EFI shell.
The files have the same nonzero sizes but are stored under a subdirectory on the ESP.

question_patterns: If you remove the initrd directives from the loader entry and pass the same initrd paths on the kernel command line, what happens?
Could you test the entry with the initrd paths moved from separate directives into the options line?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: That works. With `initrd /intel-ucode.img` and `initrd /initramfs-linux.img` in the loader entry I get the error, but with `options initrd=/intel-ucode.img initrd=/initramfs-linux.img ...` the system boots.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Moving the initrd paths to the kernel command line makes no difference; it fails with the same error.

edges.comment: Messages c0-c2 on the reporter's Dell R420: the reporter checked the actual ESP files in the EFI shell and tested the alternative command-line form. This is a configuration probe that also provides a temporary workaround, so it remains a clarification-only edge.

question_patterns: Could you build and boot the provided debug branch using the original loader initrd directives and share its console output?
Please retry with the updated diagnostic branch and photograph everything it prints before stopping.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Here is the console output from the diagnostic build. This run used the fallback initrd and ended with Bad Buffer Size. The regular initrd fails through the loader directives too.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The diagnostic build handles both initrds and boots normally without printing a read error.

edges.comment: Messages c3-c7, reporter's machine: the reporter tested participant1's diagnostic branch after it was actually committed. The screenshot is raw firmware/read output; interpreting which read is defective remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you run the proposed efi=nochunk probe with the large fallback initrd and report exactly what appears during boot?
Please test efi=nochunk with the large fallback initrd and photograph the result.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The kernel-side test with the large initrd also reaches a Bad Buffer Size failure. I attached the boot screen.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The efi=nochunk probe with the large fallback initrd boots successfully every time, while only systemd-boot's file read fails.
The same Bad Buffer Size output occurs with a slightly different fallback initrd size.

edges.comment: Messages c8-c14, reporter's Dell R420: participant1 requested the efi=nochunk probe. The reporter initially reproduced the failure; a later run used the smaller regular initrd and happened to work, so that later observation does not invalidate the large-fallback-initrd result.

question_patterns: Could you run the diagnostic branch that automatically tests a range of initrd read sizes and send the complete console output?
Please boot the chunk-size test and capture every page of its output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran it through PiKVM. The output was split across four screenshots, but I tried to capture the whole sequence of tested sizes and results.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every tested read size fails, including the smallest sizes.
The boundary in the raw output shifts slightly between runs, but the smaller tested sizes consistently succeed.

edges.comment: Messages c19-c22, reporter's machine: the reporter supplied only the raw size-bisection screens. Participant1 inferred from those screens that reads up to 16 MiB worked and that a handle was problematic after EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE; those conclusions are not placed in the reporter's answer.

solution.intent: Attempt a large read first, then recover from Bad Buffer Size by reopening the initrd and retrying with smaller chunked reads.
solution.concrete_example: On EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE, close and reopen the initrd file and retry the operation in smaller chunks.

edges.comment: Messages c22-c29, reporter's machine: participant1 implemented a reopen-and-retry candidate and the reporter tested it. It still produced the same Bad Buffer Size error; subsequent debugging also showed anomalous behavior around the reopened handle. This implementation strategy was falsified.

question_patterns: Can you run the latest debug build, capture the expected and returned sizes and SHA-256 output, and compare it with sha256sum?
Please rebuild in debug mode, boot the diagnostic image, and send both the boot output and the local hash output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I rebuilt it in debug mode. The first screenshot contains the expected and returned size plus the SHA-256 printed during boot; the second contains the follow-up output and my local comparison.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The reopened read returns the full expected size and its SHA-256 exactly matches sha256sum.

edges.comment: Messages c30-c36, reporter's Dell R420: after build-instruction clarification, the reporter produced raw expected-size, returned-size, and hash output. Participant1 concluded from it that the reopened firmware handle silently truncated the file; that diagnosis is reserved for the final solution's engineer inference.

question_patterns: Please test the latest candidate build with your original loader entry and tell me what you see.
Can you retry the updated build using the same initrd directives from your original report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Tested it with the original setup. It works like a charm.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The updated candidate still stops with Bad Buffer Size on the same entry.

edges.comment: Messages c36-c39, reporter's system: participant1 revised the candidate after interpreting the size/hash diagnostics, and the reporter later confirmed successful boot. The question deliberately does not reveal the candidate's implementation.

solution.intent: Make systemd-boot load initrds using bounded chunked reads from the outset, matching the kernel's firmware-compatibility strategy instead of attempting one oversized read or reopening a poisoned handle.
solution.concrete_example: Read each initrd in small bounded chunks from the original file handle. Do not first issue a whole-file read, and do not depend on reopening the file after EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE, because this firmware can return a truncated view from the reopened handle.
solution.inference_hint: Engineers inferred from the chunk-size bisection that the Dell firmware accepts bounded reads but returns EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE for oversized reads. They then inferred from the expected-size and SHA diagnostics that reopening after the failed read can expose a silently truncated file. These conclusions were not stated by the reporter; the reporter supplied console screenshots and confirmed whether each candidate booted.

edges.comment: Technical resolution from c36-c39: systemd-boot was changed to use chunked reads consistently, as the kernel does for firmware with limited EFI file-read sizes. The reporter confirmed the corrected candidate worked. Later backport requests and unrelated deployment reports are logistics or separate users and are not part of this reporter's diagnostic chain.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the Dell R420's buggy EFI FAT/file implementation rejects oversized initrd reads with EFI_BAD_BUFFER_SIZE, and a handle reopened after such a failure can return a silently truncated file.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: nonempty ESP files, successful kernel-command-line workaround, failure of the efi=nochunk probe with the large initrd, the chunk-size test output, and the size/hash diagnostics.
The fix must load initrds in bounded chunks from the outset, following the kernel's compatibility behavior rather than relying on one whole-file read.
Must not recommend the reopen-after-failed-read strategy as the fix; it was tested and the same error remained, with later diagnostics showing the reopened file data was unreliable.
The kernel-command-line initrd method may be described as a temporary workaround, but it must not replace the systemd-boot chunked-read fix.
Must have the reporter verify a build containing the corrected behavior before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Linux server administrator. Comfortable with Arch chroots, systemd-boot configuration, EFI shell use, custom systemd builds, PiKVM, and testing diagnostic branches, but less familiar with Meson and not initially comfortable drawing conclusions from firmware-level C behavior.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative, informal, and persistent. Provides screenshots and exact loader configurations, promptly reports unexpected outcomes, admits uncertainty, and is willing to rebuild and test multiple diagnostic candidates.
